title: Cadillac celebrates 125 years with the Escalade-V - The Manual
content: The Cadillac Escalade has been a symbol for decades. When you think about those who made it out of the neighborhood and into the more affluent parts of your home, you think of them in a Caddy. The Cadillac image has always been the go-to for those who want to showcase their success and their ability to rise above the average. The Escalade became the harbinger of wealth when it became the status symbol of the urban and hip hop cultures. Now the Escalade is the vessel Cadillac is using to celebrate 125 years with the Escalade-V. Every soul deserves a shot at a Cadillac, but not everyone should be guaranteed a Cadillac.” — Ben Stein This is the first in a collector’s series celebrating over a century of iconic luxury. The new Escalade-V comes with a slew of features. The most unique and one I would show off at every turn is the custom VIN. How many times have you been able to fill out paperwork and had your VIN memorized? Never? Me either…other features include: “The Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series celebrates Cadillac’s heritage and our uncompromising approach to performance luxury,” said Kristian Aquilina, Vice President, Global Cadillac. “From its exclusive design to its highly limited availability, this special edition gives collectors a distinctive way to celebrate Cadillac’s legacy while looking ahead to its future.” Santorini Blue holds an important place in the evolution of Cadillac V-Series design. Inspired by the blue within the V-Series emblem’s Mondrian pattern, the color was developed as a visual link between the fifth-generation V-Series and the Cadillac V-Series. R race car. First introduced on the Cadillac Project GTP concept, Santorini Blue has since appeared across V-Series race cars, road cars and concept vehicles, including the Petit Pataud and Le Monstre Collector Series editions. A Porsche is one of the most recognizable cars on the road. You always know when you are looking at one. So, it stands to reason that people love them, right? Of course they do. But loving a car and knowing how to drive one are very different. What is it that Ja Rule said in The Fast and the Furious? “We know a few things. And one of the things we knows is, it isn’t how you stand by your car, it is how to drive your car. You better learn that.” How do you learn to drive a Porsche? At the Porsche Track Experience, which has offered programs on everything from a single-day basics class up to a three-day advanced course. Now, the team behind PTX is expanding into new offerings for the car. Authenticity. It is what we are looking for nowadays as consumers. Thirty years ago, we looked for brand names. We strived for status and letting all those around us see that what we wore, where we lived, where we dined, and finally, what we drove, symbolized our success in life. Then all of that started to stumble, and every industry felt the recession. Of course, the recession was temporary, but the effects of it were not. What we started to look for after that was something real. We realized that stuff…was just stuff. Now, when I look at cars, or suits, or restaurants, I ask myself: What is this going to make me feel? That is what the new Porsche Mission S does; it makes me feel like vintage New York and the upstate escape. If you have ever been to a Formula 1 race, you probably know these machines are the pinnacle of performance. These super machines are some of the most amazing creations in the mechanical world and are a marvel to watch scream around the courses around the world during the F1 season. But how much power do they have? More specifically, how much horsepower pulls that thing around the track?

title: Montana State OL Titan Fleischmann honored as William V. Campbell Trophy finalist - MontanaSports.com
content: BOZEMAN — Montana State offensive lineman Titan Fleischmann became one of 16 finalists for the National Football Foundation's 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy, the NFF announced on Wednesday. As a Campbell Trophy finalist, Fleischmann receives an $18,000 post-graduate scholarship  and membership on the 2026 NFF National Scholar-Athlete Class Presented by Fidelity Investments. The finalists were chosen from a record 206 semifinalists nationwide across all NCAA divisions and NAIA. “Only 18 players at all levels of college football are selected for this honor,” said MSU head coach Brent Vigen. “Titan certainly embodies this award for his achievements on the field and academically, but his perseverance and leadership set him apart.” Fleischmann is the third Bobcat selected since 2021, making Montana State one of two teams with that number of recipients in that span. Oregon, whose quarterback Dante Moore is on the 2026 team, is the other. MSU is one of seven programs below the Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS) level with at least seven all-time selections. One the most accomplished student-athletes in Bobcat football history, Fleischmann holds a bachelor’s degree in political science (3.81 cumulative grade point average out of 4.0), and a master’s degree in coaching science. He is working toward a master’s degree in family financial planning. Last season, he became the first Bobcat offensive lineman to earn first-team All-America and first-team College Sports Communicators (CSC) academic All-America honors in the same year. “This award means, to me, an accumulation of a lot of hard work and the long process of figuring it out,” he said. “But mostly I’m grateful for the support system I’ve had since I started this journey of football, from my freshman year of high school until now. “All the coaches I’ve had, my parents, my family, my coaches here, the community here, this award is a way of representing everybody in my support system.” During his time as a starter in the past two-plus seasons, Fleischmann has anchored one of the top offensive lines in the Football Championship Subdivision (FCS). Montana State won the 2025 FCS national championship with Fleischmann starting all 16 games, while the Cats averaged 37.9 points and 226.2 rushing yards per game. Fleischmann joins former teammates Troy Andersen (2021) and Brody Grebe (2024) as recent selections. Other Bobcats honored by the NFF: Rich Brady (1990), Derrick Isackson (1989), Ryan Johnson (2002) and Anders Larsson (1988). “Those guys were old guys (in the Bobcat program) when I was a young buck,” Fleischmann said. “I looked up to them. I remember asking Troy Andersen when I was a freshman, ‘How did you do all that you did?’ And he said, ‘Consistency. title: Cadillac Celebrates Its 125 Birthday With The $239,000 Escalade-V Collector Series, Only Available In White Or Black - Jalopnik
content: Cadillac is one of the oldest automakers that's still in business, with its origins dating back to 1902. That means it's turning the ripe old age of 125-years-old in 2027, and on Thursday, Cadillac announced it's launching an Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series to celebrate the occasion. I'm guessing that the designers of this not-so-special edition were inspired by black-and-white photos that were taken in 1902, since this Caddy is only offered in black or white — exclusive Midnight Stone Frost and Vibrant White Tricoat, to be more accurate. In fact, the only actual color on these dapper Caddy daddymobiles is a bright shade of Santorini Blue, which adorns the seatbelts and stitching, as well as a similar blue on the brake calipers and key fob. You may be thinking that such minimal changes must also come at a minimal cost, but you're wrong. Very wrong, in fact, since the 2027 Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series starts at approximately $239,000. Ouch. Exterior touches that make the 125th Anniversary Collector Series special include unique forged 24-inch wheels, and a carbon-fiber grille surround, rear bumper insert, mirror caps, and engine cover. It also gets heritage-themed puddle lamps, a two-tone interior in Black and Sheer Gray, illuminated sill plates, interior badges, and special floor mats. Cadillac chose to sprinkle Santorini Blue around the interior because it has appeared on V-Series race cars, as well as V-Series road cars and concepts. A base 2027 Cadillac Escalade-V starts at $172,195, so going for one of these special editions adds an additional $66,805 on top of that before dealer markups. To put that into perspective, that's enough to buy a Cadillac CT5-V (though not the mind-blowingly awesome Blackwing) and still have thousands of dollars left over. At least the Cadillac stans who buy these special editions will own a very exclusive truck, since Cadillac will only build 252 of these Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series for the U.S. and Canada. Buyers will be able to select their VIN and serial number, and each color will have vehicles labeled 1902-2027, which is strange since that would add up to 250 units, not the 252 Cadillac has planned. If you have a quarter-mil burning a hole in your pocket and want to fill it with a "special" Cadillac Escalade-V, the 125th Anniversary Collector Series is available for ordering now.

title: 2027 Cadillac Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series Interior And Exterior Picture Gallery - Top Speed
content: Cadillac turns 125 with its rarest Escalade yet: a $239,000 Escalade-V Collector Series limited to 252 units, each with a serialized VIN. Cadillac is turning 125, and it’s marking the occasion with the rarest     Escalade it has ever built. Unveiled ahead of the United States Grand Prix in Austin, the 2027 Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series is the first Escalade to join Cadillac’s Collector Series, a lineup of limited editions that until now belonged to V-Series sedans like the CT5-V Blackwing. Production is capped at just 252 units across two exclusive finishes, with each color getting vehicles serialized from 1902 to 2027, one for every year of Cadillac’s history. Buyers can even pick their own VIN and serial number. Inside, Cadillac has given the Escalade-V a mix of contrasting materials, commemorative details, and exclusive accents meant to match the rarity of the exterior. The star of the cabin is a color: Santorini Blue. It’s the defining interior accent of this special edition, and it carries a lot of meaning for Cadillac’s performance brand. The shade was inspired by the blue found in the Mondrian-style pattern of the V-Series emblem. Cadillac developed it as a visual link between the fifth-generation V-Series road cars and the V-Series.R race car. Santorini Blue first appeared on the Cadillac Project GTP concept. Since then, it has shown up on V-Series race cars, road cars, and concept vehicles, including the Petit Pataud and Le Monstre Collector Series editions. In the Escalade-V, it’s applied as stitching across a Black and Sheer Gray two-tone interior. The blue thread stands out against the darker upholstery without overwhelming the Escalade’s luxury feel. The color also extends to the seat belts, which are finished in Santorini Blue. It’s a small touch, but one that’s hard to miss every time someone climbs aboard. Illuminated sill plates mark the anniversary as soon as the doors open, while exclusive interior badging reminds occupants they’re sitting in one of only 252 examples. Rounding out the package are premium floor mats designed specifically for the Collector Series and an exclusive blue key fob, so the anniversary theme follows owners even before they step inside. The Escalade-V already has plenty of road presence, but the 125th Anniversary Collector Series adds a set of details that make it stand apart from the regular model. Cadillac describes the exterior as a mix of form, finish, and performance-inspired touches. It starts with the paint. Buyers get two choices: an exclusive Midnight Stone Frost and Vibrant White Tricoat, both picked to play up the Escalade-V’s imposing size. We want to hear from you. title: Gibson Releases 50th Anniversary Tom Petty Flying V Guitars in Five Finishes - 94.7 WCSX
content: Gibson launched a limited-edition 50th Anniversary Tom Petty Flying V guitar. The design draws from the Heartbreakers logo on the band’s self-titled 1976 debut album, per Guitar.com. Gibson will build… Gibson launched a limited-edition 50th Anniversary Tom Petty Flying V guitar. The design draws from the Heartbreakers logo on the band's self-titled 1976 debut album, per Guitar.com. Gibson will build just 50 guitars in each of five finishes, so only 250 will exist worldwide. Gibson calls the set the "Flying Five." The finishes are Gainesville Gold, Graphite Metallic, Heartbreaker Red, Pearl White Metallic, and Pelham Blue. Each wears a gloss nitrocellulose lacquer coat. Prices start at $2,799 in the U.S. and £2,499 in the U.K., according to MusicRadar. A Gibson hardshell case comes with every guitar. Mahogany makes up the body and neck. The neck has a SlimTaper profile. The rosewood fretboard has a 12-inch radius, 22 medium jumbo frets, and acrylic dot inlays. Up top, the headstock carries a mother-of-pearl Gibson logo, Grover Rotomatic tuners, and a Graph Tech nut. A Heartbreaker 50th truss rod cover sits on the front. On the back, you'll find a reproduction of Tom Petty's signature. Two '70s Tribute humbucker pickups are hand-wired to separate volume controls, a master tone control with an Orange Drop capacitor, and a three-way pickup selector. The hardware is gold-plated. It includes an aluminum Nashville Tune-O-Matic bridge and a Stop Bar tailpiece. Gold Top Hat knobs, a three-ply white pickguard, and a cream toggle switch cap finish the build. "The Heartbreakers logo has been part of the band's identity since the first album, so seeing Gibson reinterpret it through the Flying V 50th anniversary edition feels overdue as they have been part of the story since the beginning," said Adria Petty, Tom Petty's daughter, in a statement, per Guitar World. "The V was an essential part of the imagery onstage for my dad as well as the band rose to fame in the 1970's. The collection honors Tom and the Heartbreakers' history while giving musicians and fans a new way to carry that spirit forward." "Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers have meant so much to so many, with timeless songs that continue to inspire us today," said Beth Heidt, Chief Marketing Officer at Gibson, added in the statement. "It is a profound honor to celebrate 50 years of that music through these instruments and this collection." Petty entered the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2002. The Gibson launch is one piece of a season packed with albums, special events, and anniversary celebrations from the band and the Tom Petty Estate. On Nov. 6, the estate will release Origins 1971-1978. This box set traces Petty's early recording years and the birth of the Heartbreakers. It mixes rare, live, and unreleased tracks with the band's first two albums. Gibson also rolled out a lifestyle line next to the guitars. The Tom Petty Estate and the Nashville brand Imogene+Willie helped make it. Fans can pick from four vintage midweight tees, outerwear, a Zippo, a bandana, a mini guitar, a snapback, a guitar strap, a pick tin, and a sticker set. One piece stands out. title: Kingdom v. Trump: There Is No Right-Wing Culture War These Two Justices Won’t Fight - Balls and Strikes
content: Want more Balls & Strikes? Sign up for our free newsletter here. This article was published in partnership with Slate. In an unsigned order on Wednesday, the Supreme Court denied the Trump administration’s request for permission to implement what is, even by the Trump administration’s standards, a remarkably barbaric element of its anti-trans agenda: a blanket denial of gender-affirming healthcare to transgender people in federal prison for the first time in three decades. Only Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito noted their dissent, because for them, nothing is more important than their solemn duty to give their favorite president whatever he wants. Shortly after taking office in January 2025, President Donald Trump issued a sweeping anti-trans executive order aimed at purging the government of “gender ideology.” This case, Trump v. Kingdom, is a legal challenge to guidance issued by the Bureau of Prisons that would effectuate the part of Trump’s order forbidding the use of federal funds for “any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.” Needless to say, losing access to care was devastating for incarcerated transgender people, who in court filings described experiencing anxiety, panic attacks, and suicidal ideation as a result of their suddenly untreated gender dysphoria. The policy of providing these inmates with the medical care they need has been in place since the first Bush administration. Fortunately for anyone who believes that the state should not have the power to torture people in its custody, lower court judges have repeatedly blocked the new guidance from taking effect. By electing to leave these orders in place, the Supreme Court indicated that, although it has been willing to sympathize with the anti-trans movement in many other contexts, sanctioning the denial of lifesaving care to incarcerated people is, at least for now, a proverbial bridge too far. By putting their disagreement on the record, Thomas and Alito are making clear that they are as eager as ever to drag the court across it. The justices do not always make their votes public in shadow docket cases, which means it is possible that one or two more justices sided with Trump here and simply chose not to say so. But through their conduct in Kingdom and other cases like it, Thomas and Alito continue to distinguish themselves as the court’s two most strident reactionaries, reflexively endorsing whatever harebrained legal theories conservative lawyers offer in service of their shared policy agenda. Whenever the other conservative justices decide that a given argument is too extreme or too ambitious, these two are right there to explain why the argument is actually correct, and to encourage activists to try again soon. Thomas and Alito have long been on the right flank of the court’s right flank: consistent opponents of abortion rights, voting rights, gun safety, and so on, and outspoken proponents of incarceration, punishment, religious supremacy, and the like. During the court’s most recent term, they voted together in 94 percent of cases on the merits docket. In their occasional speeches and public appearances, they come off as pretty generic Republican men of a certain age, airing all the usual grievances about the perils of cancel culture, the evils of progressivism, and anyone who would have the temerity to question their integrity in public. What distinguishes Thomas and Alito from the other conservatives, though, is how frequently they end up castigating their more junior colleagues for their timidity. In April 2025, for example, when the court blocked the Trump administration from deporting hundreds of people without notice to a torture prison in a country that wasn’t even home, Alito, joined by Thomas, wrote a dissent blasting the court for “hastily and prematurely” granting “legally questionable” relief “literally in the middle of the night.” In May 2026, they were the only justices who dissented from the court’s stay of a lower court order that would have severely limited the availability of abortion medication. In his opinion, Alito described this result as a “remarkable” enabling of a “scheme to undermine” the court’s decision in Dobbs—essentially scolding the conservatives for allowing states to restrict abortion, but then being too chickenshit to give those restrictions teeth. The emerging Alito-and-Thomas jurisprudence reflects not just a substantive alignment with Trump and the Republican Party, but a worldview shaped by themes, tropes, and conspiracy theories that dominate the conservative media ecosystem. The pair has written dissents downplaying police violence against Black people, for example, and emphasizing the lurid details of crimes to suggest that people convicted of them should have fewer legal rights. In May, when Florida Republicans tried to file a stunt lawsuit challenging California’s policies for issuing commercial driver’s licenses to undocumented people, Thomas and Alito argued that the court needed to hear the case because if Florida were a sovereign nation (heaven help us all), it might try to resolve the dispute with armed force. Dissenting in a criminal law case earlier this year, they mourned the court’s willingness to “intervene at the request of a convicted murderer” while “routinely” withholding relief from “law-abiding Americans” in other, unrelated cases that, in Thomas’s and Alito’s view, the court should have agreed to hear. Finally, Thomas and Alito have been outspoken dissenters whenever the court chooses not to join the culture-war fray with the zeal that the two of them would prefer. When the court passed on the case of a student disciplined for wearing a transphobic T-shirt to school, for example, they warned that the court was enabling “censorship.” When it passed on a legal challenge to a race-neutral school admissions policy, they described the court’s “willingness to swallow” the lower court decision as “hard to understand.” When it declined to rule on school policies that protect transgender students, they criticized the court for ducking a question of “great and growing national importance.” And when it declined to decide whether parents have a “fundamental” legal right to be involved in a child’s decision to seek abortion care, Thomas and Alito wrote separately to make clear that the result was not a “rejection of the argument.” Perhaps the cleanest illustration of Thomas and Alito’s loyalties came just last month, when the court issued an unsigned order preventing Trump from imposing onerous restrictions on mail-in voting before the 2026 midterm elections. In dissent, Thomas and Alito asserted that the proposed rules were necessary to ferret out “election fraud,” a conspiracy theory of which Alito is alarmingly fond. They also argued that the decision would cause Trump “irreparable harm” because it dealt a “serious setback to the Executive’s goals.” For Thomas and Alito, the legal interests of millions of people who want to participate in democracy next month were apparently not a factor worth meaningfully considering. For all that this court’s six-justice conservative supermajority has accomplished in recent years, it is still not enough for Thomas and Alito. At 78 and 76, respectively, neither man retired before the midterms, a choice that would have preserved the power of Trump and this Republican-controlled Senate to nominate and confirm their successor(s). What this suggests is that Thomas and Alito do not view cases like Dobbs as the capstone to their careers. They view themselves as stewards of the movement that led to Dobbs, and are eager to lay the groundwork for the next generation of ideologues working to use the legal system to implement their policy preferences. Even when they lose, what Thomas and Alito are doing in cases like Kingdom is applying constant rightward pressure to the law, encouraging activists to keep filing new cases, workshopping new legal theories, and offering new arguments. As the old saying goes, five votes can do anything at the Supreme Court. When the conservative legal movement knows it has two in the bag, three more never feels like too much of an ask. title: Cadillac's Escalade-V Collector Series Retails For $239,000, But Expect To Pay WAY More - CarScoops
content: Only 252 copies of this rare Escalade-V will be built Are you a fan of Cadillac? Are you a huge Cadillac fan? Are you a YUGE fan who already has some great Cadillac metal in your garage but wants something even more unique? Well, Cadillac has some great news for you. To celebrate the brand's 125th birthday, it is offering the 2027 Cadillac Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series. It's the first in the Escalade Collector Series and will feature unique options for each of the 252 units the company will offer for sale. It starts with the V Series powertrain: a 682-horsepower supercharged V8 that also generates 652 lb-ft of stump-pulling torque. You won't be doing tree work with this luxury SUV, though, because it has unique 24-inch forged wheels and carbon-fiber accents around the exterior. The exterior also has blue brake calipers and dark-finish badging. Even the light-up puddle lamps have a special V8 design for this series. Santorini Blue, an excellent hue from the V-Series emblem that links the street cars to the V-Series.R race car, appears throughout the interior. That includes the seat belts and the stitching. Additional interior changes include exclusive badging, premium floor mats, and an exclusive blue key fob. The overall interior itself is bathed in black and Sheer Gray two-tone materials. Buyers can start placing orders today and will be able to choose between Midnight Stone Frost or Vibrant White Tricoat exterior paint; plus, they'll be able to select their VIN and serial number, which makes each owner's vehicle even more unique to them. We like it better than some other custom Escalades. Of course, for all this performance and exclusivity, interested buyers will have to shell out at least $239,000 (that MSRP includes with delivery charge). With only 252 being made, the company will certainly sell out, but Cadillac reminds us that "The dealer sets final price." But is there too high a price to pay to prove you are Cadillac's most loyal fan?

title: Fighting Zombie Laws: Inside Fund Texas Choice v. Deski - scalawagmagazine.org
content: WE'RE DREAMING UP ABOLITIONIST FUTURES. Help us share our vision. Texas abortion funds help people travel out of state for abortion care in states without deadly, restrictive bans. The funds buy plane tickets, book hotel rooms, coordinate childcare, and cover the cost of the procedure. No one at these abortion funds performs abortions or prescribes abortion medication. They help people access the reproductive healthcare that Texas law does not and cannot reach. Immediately after Roe v. Wade fell in 2022, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced that the state's pre-Civil War "zombie laws" were back in effect. These "zombie laws" refer to statewide abortion bans passed before the Civil War that sat dormant for roughly a century—never formally repealed, but never enforced. When Roe was overturned, Paxton argued these bans were suddenly live again, and that anyone who "furnishes the means" for an abortion could be prosecuted under them. Soon after Paxton's advisory, many Texas abortion funds went dark. One by one, the organizations that made up the Texas abortion access network stopped answering requests, stopped booking travel, and stopped funding healthcare. September 1, 2026, marked the fifth anniversary of Texas Senate Bill 8 (SB 8), also known as the Texas Heartbeat Act, effectively banning abortions after six weeks of pregnancy. Since SB 8 went into effect in 2021, maternal deaths in Texas have increased by 56 percent, sepsis rates have risen by 50 percent, and infant… Paxton's attempted revival of the "zombie laws" didn't require a single prosecution to do its damage—only the belief that prosecution would occur. A law that hasn't been used in nearly a hundred years is now being pointed at people who believe they're following the rules—and nobody can say for certain who's right. If the funds can't tell where the line is, based on what's being reported and what elected officials are saying, the people they exist to serve can't either, which is a short step to believing Texans are all out of options. In August of 2022, Fund Texas Choice and several other Texas abortion funds sued Paxton and a class of county and district attorneys, seeking affirmation that this work—helping Texans travel out of state for legal abortion care—is not a crime. In February 2023, a federal district judge issued a preliminary injunction in the abortion funds' favor. The same ruling, however, dismissed Paxton from the case. The judge reasoned that because the funds' work happens outside Texas, Paxton had no authority to prosecute it—so the threats that had shut down the network were, legally speaking, ones he never had the power to carry out. That reasoning put the funds in an impossible position. The Attorney General of Texas had promised, publicly, to oversee the criminalization of their work. They had no way to know if he meant it, and no reason to assume he didn't. But when they sued over the threat, the court told them he was never the right person to answer for it. With Paxton out of the case, the funds' only remaining path to a final ruling ran through the local and county prosecutors—until Mi Familia Vota v. Ogg (2024). Senate Bill 4, the proposed legislation introduced the day before the Annunciation House lawsuit, would change the landscape of humanitarian work at the border and shift some of the legal pretenses of Paxton and his allies into legal reality. In that separate case, the Fifth Circuit set a new, extraordinarily high bar for individuals who initiate these kinds of lawsuits: they must show that the government official they are suing has both a "specific enforcement duty" and a "demonstrated enforcement intent." That a government official has the power to cause harm is not enough either. Using that standard, Texas moved to dismiss the prosecutors too—arguing that they had never expressed any intent to criminalize the funds or their workers, only that they had the power to. So: Paxton had the threats, but not the power, and the prosecutors had the power, but not the threats. Under Ogg, that symmetry could leave the funds with no one left to sue. The struggles for a free Palestine and bodily autonomy are deeply intertwined. What reproductive health, rights, and justice organizations are unwilling to risk in solidarity with Palestine mirrors the limitations within their movement that inhibit their solidarity with all people seeking abortion care, and those who support them, as anti-abortion criminalization escalates across the country.… The implications of Ogg reach well past Texas. The mechanisms at work in this case—private enforcement, zombie statutes, the strategic use of ambiguity—are being deployed in statehouses across the country. If the funds lose here, their defeat will serve as a warning to everyone else: that a state can make a law real without ever enforcing it, and the people on the other end have no way to challenge it until the harm has already arrived. Anna Rupani, Executive Director of Fund Texas Choice, described what it felt like to sit in the courtroom during oral arguments back on August 31. Being there, she said, was validating—even though nothing was decided that day. "I think just being there, even though it's not over, was really validating. One of the justices on the panel, as a former prosecutor himself, seemed to agree that we as Texans deserve to know exactly what a crime is as a matter of principle. We shouldn't have to guess whether threats to criminalize us are serious. The state owes us that clarity up front." What the funds are asking for is rooted in a principle older than any abortion statute: due process requires that a criminal law be clear enough for an ordinary person to know what it prohibits. The funds aren't asking the court to declare abortion legal in Texas. The funds are asking the court to say, plainly, that helping someone travel for legal care is not a crime—and that the state cannot decide otherwise based on political whim. The legal principle the funds are invoking is not an abstraction. Texas has spent the last several years demonstrating what happens when no court is positioned to enforce it. Last year, a Houston-area midwife was indicted on fifteen felonies over allegations that she continued to provide abortion care despite state bans. Her prosecution sits alongside Texas's own lawsuits against the cities of Austin and San Antonio for providing financial assistance to residents traveling out of state for abortion, as examples of the same posture: the state treating care and compassion as a public safety threat. President Biden promised to 'undo the damage that Trump has done,' but that work falls on organizers' shoulders. Earlier this year, several of the defendants involved in a Prairieland-area protest against ICE were sentenced to 30 to 100 years in federal prison. Their sentences were explicitly framed as sending a cruel, chilling deterrent message to their fellow Texans organizing against the continued caging of their immigrant neighbors. In the current federal judicial climate, Texas's criminal enforcement machinery is capable of redefining any activity it dislikes as a serious crime—from midwifery to helping someone cross state lines for abortion care to political protest. Rupani connected the recent sentencing of the Prairieland defendants directly to the stakes of her own case. "It's not very hard to see that, in our current political climate, furnishing the means could mean anything on a given day, whatever the powers that be don't want you to do, they're gonna find a way to make it so that you can't do it. We can't just act like that is not a constant, looming threat. It is absolutely not hypothetical." Our anchoring question is this: Can you be an accomplice to Reproductive Justice while wielding the power to incarcerate, separate families, and deny medical care—as long as you agree to look the other way on one specific charge? If the Fifth Circuit ultimately dismisses this lawsuit and the Ogg standard is upheld, abortion funds, bail funds, mutual aid networks, and even legal defense groups could face a shared, grim fate. As long as a state legislature passes a law with criminal penalties attached—whether it's been enforced a hundred times or hasn't been used in a hundred years—anyone challenging it must first be directly and severely harmed before they can sue. "They want a world where the only way to challenge a law is to let it put someone in handcuffs first." That loop is not self-sustaining. It depends on people—the ones who decide whether to file charges, whether to open an investigation, whether to let a threat stay a threat. The funds don't expect a final ruling in their case until at least 2027, but some of the people who will decide whether they can operate in the meantime are on the ballot this November. The midterms will dominate the next several weeks of news coverage, and most of that coverage will focus on the U.S. Congress and the composition of each state's legislature. But Fund Texas Choice v. Deski is a reminder that the architecture of abortion criminalization isn't contained to Washington or the state capitol. It lives, in large part, in the hands of people whose names the average Texan never learns. The Texas legislature has already passed a series of bills aimed at criminalizing help with abortion access. That these laws are on the books at all is already injustice. But a law on the books is not the same as a law in effect. Whether a statute becomes a prosecution—or a chill, or nothing at all—depends on enforcement, and enforcement is a choice made by individuals: district attorneys, attorneys general, judges. People who answer to Texas voters in ways that are easy to overlook when the spotlight is always fixed on Washington or Austin. If candidates committed to making an example out of abortion funds take office at any level, the pressure to do so intensifies and reverberates at all levels of government. But the same discretion that Paxton used to shut down this support network is the discretion a future Attorney General could use to refuse to. That is not a partisan observation—it is a description of how a certain kind of governance works, one that gets the least attention yet often has the highest stakes. First, Ogg raised the bar for suing officials who threaten enforcement but haven't yet carried it out. Then prosecutors learned to describe their own power without acknowledging any intention to use it—a rhetorical discipline that now functions as a legal shield. The result is a closed loop: officials can threaten, but the threats are too vague to challenge; the people threatened must wait to be harmed, but the harm is designed to arrive without warning. In this loop, the state's most effective tool is the credible possibility of prosecution, suspended indefinitely over people's heads, immune from review. Texas' governance strategy is already traveling. SB 8's bounty-hunter mechanism has inspired copycat legislation in Florida, Ohio, Arkansas, and Alabama. The Prairieland sentences, which converted protest into decades of prison time, offer a model for anyone who wants to treat dissent itself as a public safety threat. Texas has long-proven that what happens here doesn't stay here, and its zombie-law maneuver will be no exception. "They're trying different things, seeing what works, seeing where they can make progress. And they'll use those tools in as many places as they can." The abortion funds didn't close because the state proved its case. They closed because the state made the case impossible to disprove. Fund Texas Choice v. Deski has become a test of whether the courts will enforce the most basic limit on state power: that before the government can call something a crime, it has to say so clearly, in advance, to everyone. "We're not just fighting for abortion funds to exist," Rupani said. "We're fighting for everyone's right to have the judicial branch work for them and have their day in court." Whatever the Fifth Circuit decides, the question it leaves Texans with is the one Paxton's "zombie law" advisory was designed to raise: If you can't even find out whether your work is a crime until it's too late, who exactly is the law protecting? Ja'Loni Owens is a Black Muslim feminist lawyer, writer and full-spectrum birth worker based in the Greater Atlanta Metro area. Ja'Loni’s legal and policy background is primarily in eliminating patriarchal violence, family policing abolition, international human rights, and bodily autonomy. title: Irene V. Anderson Winka (87) of Flora - 979 XFM
content:
Published on October 22, 2026 11:56 am 
Last Updated on October 22, 2026 1:11 pm Irene V. Anderson Winka, 87, of Flora, Illinois, passed away on October 19, 2026, at Carle Richland Memorial Hospital in Olney. She was a devoted wife, mother, grandmother, and great grandmother, and a woman of strong Catholic faith. Visitation will be held from 5 until 7 p.m. on Friday, October 30, 2026, at Frank & Bright Funeral Home in Flora, with a Rosary at 7 p.m. Visitation will continue from 9 until 10 a.m. on Saturday, October 31, at St. Stephen Catholic Church, where a Mass of Christian Burial will be celebrated at 10 a.m. with Father Patrick Peter officiating. Burial will follow in St. Stephen Cemetery. In keeping with her love of reading, memorial donations may be made to the Flora Public Library and will be accepted at the funeral home. To share a condolence or memory, visit: www.frankandbright.com.
Irene was born on November 9, 1938, in Bible Grove Township to the late King Anderson and Esther (Dueker) Anderson. She graduated from North Clay Community High School in Louisville in 1956. On January 14, 1961, Irene married Raymond R. “Ray” Winka at St. Stephen Catholic Church in Flora. Together they raised five children and
shared 58 years of marriage before Ray’s passing in 2019. Irene spent her working years at Samuel Music in Effingham, the Flora Chamber of Commerce, and KSH/DRG Plastics, where she served as plant secretary. She was also a familiar face in Tupperware sales for many years. Irene’s faith was a cornerstone of her life. She was a faithful member of St. Stephen Catholic Church and its St. Anne’s Altar Society. One of her proudest accomplishments was playing the organ at Mass. Family was Irene’s greatest joy. She loved cooking for her family and made sure every holiday and birthday was properly celebrated. She treasured family vacations, lent a hand in Ray’s strawberry patch, and could often be found at the table playing Scrabble or pinochle with her children and grandchildren. Scrabble was a particular favorite, and her knack for spelling had earned her a spelling bee award back in grade school. In quieter moments, she enjoyed a good book. Irene is survived by her children, Mike Winka and wife, Tina, of Flora, Debbie “Deb” Keller of Olney, Mark Winka and wife, Janet, of Xenia, Tracy Winka of St. Louis, Missouri, and Brent Winka of Flora; eight grandchildren, Lindsay Keller Andrews, Josh Winka, Matthew Winka, Hailey Winka Tuggle, Ryan Winka, Nicholas Winka, Brooke Winka, and Jordan Winka; and four great grandchildren, Keller, Harper, Nora, and Everley. She was preceded in death by her parents; her husband, Raymond; and her sister, Mildred Garrison.
Irene will be remembered for her faith, her love of a good book, and the warmth she brought to every family gathering. © Copyright 2026 Premier Broadcasting. All rights reserved.         206 S Willow, Effingham, IL 62401 – Phone: (217) 347-5518 – Fax: (217) 347-5519

title: $325,000 125th Anniversary is Cadillac's most expensive Escalade-V ever - Driving

Or sign-in if you have an account. If you’ve ever contemplated spending your hard-earned dollars on a brand-new Cadillac Escalade-V, the time to do it is most certainly not now. Well, that is, unless you’d love to spend some $325,000 on an exclusive 125th Anniversary Collector Series edition. And, hey, maybe you would, since you see the appeal in being one of only 252 people in Canada and the U.S. that can call this anniversary edition your own. Is that kind of exclusivity enough to get you into a Caddy that costs over $300k? Let’s think about this logically, just for a second. The regular-schmegular Cadillac Escalade has a starting price of $120,799 for the 2026 model year, and the top Platinum trims ring in at $158,399 before fees. The Escalade IQ, the all-electric version of the popular Caddy, costs between $157,399 and $177,499 before fees. The prices keep climbing, right? If you want more power, you can move up the Escalade-V, which starts at a whopping $211,099 for 2026. But why in the world is the limited anniversary edition so much more? As per Cadillac, this special version “combines the commanding presence of Escalade; the performance character of V-Series; and design details created for collectors.” But what do those design details really entail? title: Is This Special Edition 2027 Cadillac Escalade-V Really Worth $239K? - MotorTrend
content:
The 2027 Cadillac Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series marks how far the American luxury automaker has come. Cadillac was founded in August 1902 and rolled out its first cars, a pair of horseless carriages powered by 10-hp single-cylinder engines, just three months later. For 2027, the American luxury brand will celebrate its founding with the Cadillac Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series, a limited-edition model with a 682-hp supercharged V-8. Anniversary models will come painted in Vibrant White Tricoat or Midnight Stone Frost, the latter of which is exclusive to this special edition. Cadillac will build 126 examples in each color with every car getting a placard dedicating it to a single year from 1902 through 2027. That means the total production run amounts to just 252 examples. You can identify these limited-edition V’s by their unique forged 24-inch wheels over blue brake calipers and the carbon-fiber grille surround, lower rear fascia, mirror caps, and engine cover. Special puddle lamps project a heritage V-8 logo onto the ground at night while the exterior badging features a dark finish. The interior is covered in black and Sheer Gray upholstery accented with Santorini Blue stitching and seat belts in a nod to the V-Series Mondrian logo. Special illuminated sill plates pay homage to Cadillac’s long and rich history of building V-8 engines. There are also premium floor mats, a blue key fob, and the requisite interior badging. To sweeten the deal, buyers have the option of choosing their own VIN. Mechanically, the 125th Anniversary Collector Series is identical to any other Escalade-V with a supercharged 6.2-liter V-8, MagneRide dampers, and all-wheel-drive. We tested an Escalade-V back in 2023 and clocked a 4.7-second run from 0–60 mph. That might not sound all that quick by today’s standards, but don’t get hung up on one number. The engine sound alone might be reason enough to own an Escalade-V. At a price of approximately $239,000, the 125th Anniversary Collector Series costs almost $69,000 more than the run-of-the-mill Escalade-V. It will be sold in both the U.S. and Canada and can be ordered through dealers now. Cadillac launched the Collector Series in 2022 with the first 250 units of the CT4-V Blackwing and the CT5-V Blackwing. Last year the automaker celebrated its entry into Formula 1 racing with a 26-car run of the CT5-V Blackwing F1 Collector Series that featured a power increase from 668 to 685 hp and an F1 logo stamped into the front doors. I fell in love with car magazines during sixth-grade silent reading time and soon realized that the editors were being paid to drive a never-ending parade of new cars and write stories about their experiences. Could any job be better? The answer was obvious to 11-year-old me.
By the time I reached high school, becoming an automotive journalist wasn’t just a distant dream, it was a goal. I joined the school newspaper and weaseled my way into media days at the Detroit auto show. With a new driver’s license in my wallet, I cold-called MotorTrend’s Detroit editor, who graciously agreed to an informational interview and then gave me the advice that set me on the path to where I am today. Get an engineering degree and learn to write, he said, and everything else would fall into place.
I left nothing to chance and majored in both mechanical engineering and journalism at Michigan State, where a J-school prof warned I’d become a “one-note writer” if I kept turning in stories about cars for every assignment. That sounded just fine by me, so I talked my way into GM’s Lansing Grand River Assembly plant for my next story.
My child-like obsession with cars started to pay off soon after. In 2007, I won an essay contest to fly to the Frankfurt auto show and drive the Saturn Astra with some of the same writers I had been reading since sixth grade. Winning that contest launched my career. I wrote for Jalopnik and Edmunds, interned at Automobile, finished school, and turned down an engineering job with Honda for full-time employment with Automobile. In the years since, I’ve written for Car and Driver, The New York Times, and now, coming full circle, MotorTrend.
It has been a dream. A big chunk of this job is exactly what it looks like: playing with cars. I’m happiest when the work involves affordable sporty hatchbacks, expensive sports cars, manual transmissions, or any technology that requires I learn something to understand how it works, but I’m not picky. title: Cadillac Just Dropped A $239,000 Escalade To Celebrate Its 125th Anniversary - CarBuzz
content: Cadillac will celebrate its 125th anniversary in 2027 after getting started in 1902. General Motors purchased the brand in 1909, and it took the reins as the automaker's flagship luxury division. Over the decades, Cadillac has had highs, like introducing its V16-powered models in 1930, and lows like the Cimarron, a basic Chevrolet Cavalier with more chrome. As part of the 125th anniversary festivities, Cadillac is introducing a special-edition Escalade-V that costs well over $200,000. Some of the touches are similar to the recently launched Escalade-V Checo Pérez Edition, which is exclusive to just 11 units for Mexico. The 125th Anniversary Collector Series focuses more on giving the Escalade-V enhanced styling rather than improving the SUV's already impressive performance. The exterior comes in either Midnight Stone Frost, which is not generally available on the Escalade-V, or the existing premium shade Vibrant White Tricoat, which generally costs $1,325. Regardless of the hue, there's a "1902-2027" badge identifying the vehicle as a special-edition model. This Escalade-V also features carbon-fiber pieces for the grille surround, engine cover, mirror caps, and lower rear fascia. It rides on 24-inch wheels with a dark finish and a multi-spoke design unique to this edition. The badges have a shadowy finish, and there are blue brake calipers. The puddle lamps show a "V8 Est. 1914" logo on the ground, in reference to when the brand introduced its first V8-powered model. Inside, all Collector Series models come in a mix of two-tone Black and Sheer Gray leather, with Santorini Blue stitching. The seat belts are also Santorini Blue. There are also illuminated sill plates and premium floor mats. Special badges indicate this is a special version of the Escalade. Despite the Collector Series' extensive price tag, Cadillac leaves the Escalade-V's powertrain alone. Not that it needs improving – it packs a supercharged 6.2-liter V8 producing 682 horsepower and 653 pound-feet of torque. The engine hooks up to a 10-speed automatic gearbox that routes power to an all-wheel-drive system. Cadillac estimates the SUV can hit 60 miles per hour in 4.4 seconds and reach a top speed of 125 miles per hour. To make the most of the power, the Escalade-V also has a specific calibration for the Magnetic Ride Control suspension. content: A Christ-centered education you can afford - Learn More A Christ-centered education you can afford - Learn More A Christ-centered education you can afford - Learn More A Christ-centered education you can afford - Learn More A Christ-centered education you can afford - Learn More A Christ-centered education you can afford - Learn More A Christ-centered education you can afford - Learn More A Christ-centered education you can afford - Learn More by Allie Greer | Oct 22, 2026 | Milligan Press Release, News MILLIGAN, Tenn. (Oct. 22, 2026) — Emmanuel Christian Seminary at Milligan welcomes Dr. Amos Yong, professor of theology and mission at Fuller Theological Seminary, to discuss ecotheology during this year’s Edwin V. Hayden Lectureship in New Testament on Nov. 4 and 5. The lectures will be held in the Mildred Welshimer Phillips Memorial Chapel in the B.D. Phillips Building and are free and open to the public. Yong’s lecture series, “Earth: Translating Ecotheology,” includes: Yong has served in a variety of leadership roles during his career at Fuller Theological Seminary. He began teaching in 2014 as professor of theology and mission. He has served as director of the School of Intercultural Studies’ Center for Missiological Research and overseen the seminary’s graduate and doctoral intercultural studies programs. In 2019, Yong was appointed dean of the School of Intercultural Studies and of the School of Theology before he was named chief academic officer for Fuller in 2020. Yong returned to faculty status in 2023 where he continues to research and write, contributing more than five dozen books and hundreds of scholarly articles over his career. Before coming to Fuller, Yong taught for nine years at Regent University School of Divinity, where the last positions he held were J. Rodman Williams Professor of Theology and dean. Prior to that, he was on the faculty at Bethel University and Bethany College of the Assemblies of God and served as a pastor. He also worked in social and health services in Vancouver, Washington. Yong’s scholarship is foundational in Pentecostal theology, interacting with both traditional theological traditions and contemporary contextual theologies. His research deals with themes such as the theologies of Christian-Buddhist dialogue, disability, hospitality, theology and science, political theology, Asian American theology, and the mission of God. Yong is a licensed minister with the International Church of the Foursquare Gospel. He is currently a senior fellow at the Center for Theological Inquiry at Princeton Theological Seminary. The Edwin V. Hayden Lectureship honors the legacy of Dr. Edwin V. Hayden, a prolific minister, writer, teacher, editor, husband and father. In addition to 18 years in vocational ministry, Hayden served as editor of the Christian Standard. In 1988, Emmanuel honored Hayden as the first recipient of the James A. Garfield Award for service to the church. Hayden’s children include Marshall Hayden, Nadyne Renner and Linda Lawson. For more information on the Edwin V. Hayden Lectureship at Emmanuel, visit ecs.milligan.edu/lectures. 1 Blowers Boulevard | PO Box 500Milligan, Tennessee 37682 | 423.461.8700

title: Leinster v Munster: Dan Sheehan's shock position change as key internationals make timely return for Irish derby - Planet Rugby
content:
Dan Sheehan (right) and Gavin Coombes (left) are both included for Saturday's Irish derby between Leinster and Munste Leinster and Munster have named their teams for Saturday’s huge Interpro clash, with both coaches welcoming back key Ireland internationals. The sides both come into the game in Dublin off the back of impressive wins in Europe last time out, with Leinster beating Clermont Auvergne 43-28 away from home while Munster edged Racing 92 33-25, and will be looking to make it two on the spin this weekend. A win for either side could also take them into the top eight of the URC table, with Leinster currently sat on eight points and Munster on nine, but a loss could see them pulled closer to the bottom as well. Leo Cullen has made four changes to his squad from that win in France last weekend, but the headlines will be taken by the shock position change of captain Dan Sheehan, who swaps hooker for number eight this weekend. This will be the first time the 28-year-old forward will start a game in the back-row and comes amid injuries to both Caelan Doris and Jack Conan. Stormers boss takes aim at English journalist for ‘preposterous’ rumour as Springboks hopeful has ‘got no interest’ Hugo Keenan starts at full-back, with brothers Tommy and Jimmy O’Brien named on the wings. Jamie Osborne comes into the midfield to partner Robbie Henshaw this weekend, while former Munsterman Joey Carbery makes his first appearance since re-joining Leinster this off-season at fly-half. Jamison Gibson-Park also comes into the side at scrum-half. Sheehan is joined by Josh van der Flier and Ryan Baird in an exciting back-row, while James Ryan and Joe McCarthy start in the locks. The aforementioned move from Sheehan sees Rónan Kelleher come into the side at hooker, joining Tadhg Furlong and Andrew Porter in the run-on front-row. title: How to watch Lech Poznán v Sunderland in the Europa League, team news, predicted line-ups and more - Yahoo Sports
content: Sunderland travel to Poland to take on the Polish Champions in their Europa League clash on Thursday night. The game will kick off at 5:45 pm UK time at the Enea Stadion. The match will be aired on TNT Sports 1 and HBO Max (UK) Brian Brobbey is still managing a hamstring problem while Dan Ballard and Romaine Mundle remain unavailable due to injury. Wilson Isidor and Thomas Meunier were both back on the grass this week but did not partake in training with the rest of the team and remain doubtful. Isidor's ongoing recovery means that young Ukrainian Timur Tutierov is expected to lead the line for Sunderland. Fellow under-21 teammates Jenson Jones, Tom Proctor and Jack Whittaker are set to be involved with the matchday squad after partaking in Wednesday's training session. The hosts are without their main striker as Allahyar Sayyadmanesh is currently injured, but while he did partake in individual training this week, he is expected to miss out on tonight's game. Poznán have further injury worries. Alex Douglas and Joao Moutinho are long-term absentees as well as 19-year-old Wojciech Mońka. Full-back Robert Gummy trained alone on Wednesday but is a doubt for the game. Regis Le Bris has spoke about Sunderland's poor start to the domestic season with his side currently sitting bottom of the Premier League. "I think this team has emotions, and this team cares a lot as well. "It's really positive to have reactions, and to try to find solutions because we still have a good team. "We know how relentless this league [Premier League] is – when you make a few mistakes, then you get punished quickly. It was the case again at Bournemouth, so it's important to understand, it's important to work together. "It's important to share ideas as well, and tell the truth with each other." Lech Poznań head coach Frederiksen has insisted that the previous two 4-0 defeats in the Europa League, at the hands of Crystal Palace and Bayer Leverkusen, do not match his team's performances. He said: "If we take into account the trip to London, we did lose heavily, but I wouldn't rate our performance as reflecting that result. "The match against Leverkusen was demanding for us, but I think they were the best team we've had the chance to play against so far. "I'd like to emphasize that we're not a team that will always focus on defence, but we want to show our style of play and not just stick to defence. We want to attack, create chances, and perform in line with our philosophy. "We're disappointed to have lost both matches and conceded eight goals, but we're still in the Europa League. We have the belief and conviction to win." Sunderland (4-3-3): Roefs; Hume, Danso, O'Nien, Methalie; Ahoka, Sadiki, Rigg; Angulo, Tutierov, Fofana. title: Leinster v Munster: Dan Sheehan switches to number eight for Aviva Stadium derby - BBC
content: Dan Sheehan will captain Ireland in next month's Nations Championship games in Caelan Doris' absence Leinster captain Dan Sheehan will start at number eight for the first time in Saturday's United Rugby Championship derby against Munster in Dublin. The Ireland hooker switches to the back row as one of four changes made by head coach Leo Cullen for the Aviva Stadium game (18:00 BST) following last weekend's 48-23 Investec Champions Cup victory over Clermont Auvergne. Ireland scrum-half Jamison Gibson-Park makes his first appearance of the season, while former Munster out-half Joey Carbery earns his first start since rejoining Leinster, with Sam Prendergast not included. Ronan Kelleher and Jamie Osborne are also drafted into the starting side, with Kelleher replacing Sheehan at hooker and Osborne joining Robbie Henshaw in midfield. The hosts are seeking consecutive URC victories after bouncing back from opening defeats by the Lions and Sharks with a convincing win over Cardiff. Leinster have collected eight points from their opening three league matches, including four bonus points. Munster, meanwhile, have made seven changes to the side that defeated Racing 92 in the Champions Cup last weekend. Shane Daly returns from injury, while Josh Wycherley, Kieran Brookes, Fineen Wycherley, Jack O'Donoghue, Alex Kendellen and Gavin Coombes are also drafted into the starting XV. Former Ireland Under-20s international Sean O'Brien switches from the wing to outside centre as he prepares to make his 50th Munster appearance. Mark Donnelly is in line for his first appearance of the season from the bench, with academy centre Gordon Wood also among the replacements. Tadhg Beirne and Craig Casey - the only Munster players in Andy Farrell's latest Ireland squad - both start. Munster have recovered from their opening URC defeat by Glasgow Warriors with a victory over the Bulls and a 26-26 draw against Ulster on October 10. title: UH donates historic Pisces V submersible to Bishop Museum - Hawaii News Now
content: HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - A deep-sea submersible that spent decades exploring the Pacific has a new home at Bishop Museum. The University of Hawaiʻi at Manoa donated Pisces V to the museum after nearly four decades of research and exploration through the Hawaiʻi Undersea Research Laboratory. UH acquired the three-person submersible in 1985. It was capable of operating at depths of up to 6,500 feet and was used to study underwater volcanoes, coral reefs and maritime heritage sites across the Pacific. Pisces V made more dives on Hawaiʻi’s active underwater volcano Kamaʻehuakanaloa than any other submersible, according to UH. It also played a role in locating historic wrecks, including a Japanese midget submarine sunk hours before the attack on Pearl Harbor and several World War II Japanese aircraft-carrying submarines off Oʻahu. “Each of these dives were unique, each different,” said longtime Pisces V pilot and HURL operations director Terry Kerby. “We discovered multiple new species and by combining submersible operations with human divers, we explored deep-sea coral ecosystems in a new way.” HURL operations changed after federal funding ended in 2012, and Pisces V later remained in storage. UH said there was no prospect of federal funding to refurbish or redeploy the vessel, prompting the decision to donate it to Bishop Museum. “The role of Bishop Museum involves telling the stories that matter to Hawai‘i and the Pacific, including stories of ocean exploration,” said museum President and CEO Kris Helgen. “We are thrilled to have the Pisces V on our campus.” Bishop Museum also holds more than 1,000 scientifically important specimens collected by the submersible over the years. Museum officials said Pisces V will now help teach visitors about ocean science, volcanology and Hawaii’s history of deep-sea exploration. Copyright 2026 Hawaii News Now. All rights reserved.

title: Mānoa: Legendary UH submersible Pisces V begins new chapter at Bishop Museum - University of Hawaii System
content:
After nearly four decades of uncovering historic mysteries of the Pacific Ocean, the deep-sea submersible Pisces V is embarking on a new journey on land. The University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa donated the legendary three-person research vessel to the Bernice Pauahi Bishop Museum, ensuring that its legacy of deep-ocean exploration, volcanic research and historic maritime discoveries will be preserved for generations to come. “The donation ensures the submersible’s storied past will be celebrated and shared with museum visitors from Hawai‘i and around the world,” said Chip Fletcher, dean of the UH Mānoa School of Ocean and Earth Science and Technology, home of the Hawaiʻi Undersea Research Laboratory (HURL). HURL operated Pisces V along with its sister submersible, Pisces IV, for decades. However, after years in storage with no prospect of federal funding for refurbishment or redeployment, UH made the decision to entrust the historic craft to the museum. In 1985, UH acquired Pisces V, anchoring HURL’s growing undersea capabilities. Its unique maneuverability, size and depth range, operating at depths up to 6,500 feet, made it the ideal platform for navigating complex terrain and gracefully exploring delicate ecosystems. “Operating as the only U.S. deep submergence facility based in the Pacific Rim, HURL’s work with Pisces V revolutionized oceanography across several fronts,” said Terry Kerby, veteran Pisces V pilot and HURL operations director. “The submersibles were fine-tuned to adapt to the demands of operating effectively in the wide range of terrain and conditions of undersea volcanoes, seamounts in Papahānaumokuākea and beyond, maritime heritage site surveys, salvage operations of lost instruments and vehicles, and decades of pipeline support for the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawai‘i Authority cold water pipe systems. It is exciting to see the Pisces V and this legacy preserved at the Bishop Museum.” Close to home, Pisces V, enabled unprecedented exploration of the seamounts and coral reefs of the Main and Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. The submersible made more dives on Hawaiʻi’s active underwater volcano, Kamaʻehuakanaloa (previously known as Lōʻihi Seamount), than any other submersible. HURL submersibles also pioneered research on mesophotic and deep-sea coral reefs off Maui and throughout the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, conducting vital impact assessments on commercial fishing damage. Throughout the Pacific basin, the submersible ferried teams of researchers on voyages of discovery to places no human had seen before. In 2005, Pisces V embarked on a five-month expedition across the Pacific, exploring active submarine volcanoes along the Kermadec Arc near New Zealand. “Each of these dives were unique, each different,” Kerby shared. “We discovered multiple new species and by combining submersible operations with human divers, we explored deep-sea coral ecosystems in a new way.” Under Kerby’s piloting, Pisces V unlocked famous historical mysteries on the ocean floor. Highlights include locating the Japanese midget submarine sunk by the USS Ward hours before the December 7, 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor, as well as locating massive World War II Japanese aircraft-carrying submarines I-400, I-401, and I-14 off Oʻahu.Preserving a legacy at Bishop Museum Though HURL’s operations changed dramatically in 2012 when funding ended, the research and technical teams preserved the Pisces V and its priceless 35-year video and biological data archive. Now, the donation to the Bishop Museum opens a vibrant new chapter. “The Museum has a long and productive history of partnership with the University of Hawai‘i and the Hawai‘i Undersea Research Laboratory,” said Richard Pyle, Senior Curator of Ichthyology and Director of Natural Sciences at Bishop Museum. “Researchers at the Museum have done many dives within these subs over the decades, and our collections hold more than 1,000 scientifically important specimens the sub has collected over the years. It’s very exciting that we can help perpetuate the incredible legacy of these submersibles, and honor the people who fortified that legacy.” In addition to sharing the history of exploration and celebrating the dedicated engineers, pilots, and support crews whose ingenuity made thousands of safe dives possible, the Pisces V’s presence at the museum will inspire future generations of explorers and spark curiosity in ocean science, volcanology, and marine heritage among visitors. “Above all, we want to make sure the important legacy of these submarines is maintained and communicated to our visitors at the Museum,” said Kris Helgen, president and CEO of Bishop Museum. “The role of Bishop Museum involves telling the stories that matter to Hawai‘i and the Pacific, including stories of ocean exploration. We are thrilled to have the Pisces V on our campus.” Though her sea days have concluded, Pisces V will continue her mission on shore—teaching visitors about the vast, dark world beneath the waves that she spent a lifetime illuminating. title: The Supreme Court Upholds Preliminary Injunction in Kingdom v. Trump,… - Human Rights Campaign
content:
by

                Aneesha Pappy
              
•
                October 21, 2026 HRC President Kelley Robinson: “This decision protects trans inmates from the administration’s attempt to steamroll constitutional rights for now, but the fight to uphold the dignity and respect our community deserves is far from over.” WASHINGTON, DC— Today, the Supreme Court upheld the lower court’s preliminary injunction in Kingdom v. Trump, blocking Trump’s executive order that prohibits the federal Bureau of Prisons from providing transition-related medical care to transgender incarcerated people in federal facilities while the case moves through the courts. Human Rights Campaign President Kelley Robinson released the following statement: “Today, trans people in federal prisons can keep getting the care they need. Denying access to critical medical care for incarcerated people simply because they are trans is discriminatory, cruel and flies in the face of our Eighth Amendment protections. Trump and MAGA extremists are obsessed with targeting our community and undermining access to essential healthcare, defying the recommendations of every major medical association in the country. This decision protects incarcerated trans people from the administration’s attempt to steamroll over constitutional rights for now, but the fight to uphold the dignity and respect our community deserves is far from over.” Kingdom v. Trump challenges an executive order issued earlier this year by Trump prohibiting the federal Bureau of Prisons from providing transition-related medical care for incarcerated transgender people in federal prisons and detention centers. The executive order also mandated the transfer of transgender women held in federal facilities to men’s facilities. With support by the ACLU, the ACLU of DC and the Transgender Law Center, the class action lawsuit was filed on behalf of three transgender inmates, arguing that the executive order violates the U.S. Constitution’s Eighth Amendment protections against “cruel and unusual punishments” by denying access to medically-necessary healthcare. In June of this year, the plaintiffs were granted a preliminary injunction blocking the enforcement of the executive order by a federal district court judge — which has now been upheld. The case will continue to be adjudicated in the District Court for the District of Columbia. From the courtroom to the classroom, from Congress to corporate America, HRC and the HRC Foundation build power through partnerships, storytelling, and action—working to create a future rooted in equity, freedom and belonging for all LGBTQ+ people. title: Beau Brungard Named NFF William V. Campbell Trophy Finalist - Youngstown State Athletics
content:
Beau Brungard Named NFF William V. Campbell Trophy Finalist YSU QB Beau Brungard has been named one of the finalists for the 2026 National Football Foundation William V. Campbell Trophy®, the National Football Foundation (NFF) & College Hall of Fame announced today. The William V. Campbell Trophy® is college football's premier scholar-athlete award that annually recognizes an individual as the absolute best in the nation for his combined academic success, football performance and exemplary leadership. This prestigious award is given to only 18 finalists across all levels of NCAA divisions including NAIA. Each finalist will receive an $18,000 postgraduate scholarship as a member of the 2026 NFF National Scholar-Athlete Class Presented by Fidelity Investments®. Brungard is one of only two players representing the FCS this year, joining him is Montana State offensive lineman, Titan Fleischmann. A dynamic dual-threat quarterback and the 2025 Walter Payton Award winner as the top player in the FCS, Beau Brungard has rewritten the Youngstown State record books while excelling in the classroom. The New Middletown, Ohio, native becomes the Penguins' second NFF National Scholar-Athlete and first since 1998. Having graduated summa cum laude in May with a degree in business administration, Brungard is currently pursuing an MBA. A two-time CSC Academic All-District selection and two-time First Team Academic All-Missouri Valley Football Conference (MVFC) honoree, he has also earned recognition on the Dean's List. A unanimous First Team All-American in 2025, Brungard also claimed the Walter Camp Foundation FCS Player of the Year Award, FCS ADA Offensive Player of the Year honors and MVFC Offensive Player of the Year accolades. A two-time First Team All-MVFC selection, he led the FCS last season in total offense (4,702 yards) and points responsible for (326), becoming the first player in FCS history to pass for more than 300 yards and rush for 200 yards in a single game. He also set the MVFC single-game rushing record for a quarterback with 264 yards against Robert Morris. Brungard continues to rewrite the YSU record books, holding career marks for total offense (10,786 yards), offensive plays (1,524) and rushing touchdowns (57) and counting. Through eight games in 2026, he has passed for 2,061 yards and 19 touchdowns while rushing for 647 yards and 11 scores. Against Indiana State on Oct. 10, he threw for a career-high 386 yards and three touchdowns while rushing for two more scores, breaking Youngstown State's all-time career rushing touchdowns record. This season, he ranks first nationally in points responsible for per game (23.0), second in total offense (338.5 yards per game), sixth in passing yards (2,061) and sixth in total points scored (68). He leads the MVFC in multiple categories, including total offense, passing yards, pass completions and rushing touchdowns. A two-year team captain, Brungard led the Penguins to the 2025 FCS Playoffs and a final No. 19 national ranking. His leadership has helped YSU earn a 6-2 record and a No. 4 AFCA national ranking. His father, Mark, quarterbacked the Penguins from 1992-95, helping YSU capture national championships in 1993 and 1994. Off the field, Brungard leads team Bible study sessions and organizes a summer youth football camp. He also mentors local children individually and represents Youngstown State at numerous community and university functions. "The Campbell Trophy represents everything right in college football," said NFF Chairman Archie Manning, whose sons Peyton (a Campbell Trophy® recipient) and Eli were NFF National Scholar-Athletes in 1997 and 2003, respectively. "These 18 finalists have competed at an extraordinary level while embracing the demands of the classroom and making a meaningful difference in their communities. They understand that success is about more than what happens on Saturdays, and we are proud to recognize them as examples of the character, discipline and leadership that make college football so special." The finalists will travel to the Bellagio Resort & Casino in Las Vegas for the 68th NFF Annual Awards Dinner Presented by Las Vegas on Dec. 8, where their accomplishments will be highlighted in front of one of the most powerful audiences in all of sports. Live during the event, one member of the class will be declared as the winner of the 37th Campbell Trophy® and have his postgraduate scholarship increased to $25,000.
